passage: In the school counsellor's small office, Abhinav's mother twisted the strap of her bag. 'Since his Nani died, he asks the same questions every night. Will you die? Will I die? Where is she? And yesterday I found him burying his toy car in a flowerpot and saying prayers. Is something wrong with him?' Mr Irfan, the counsellor, listened. 'This is very common. Repeating questions and playing it out is how children his age make sense of a loss. Short, honest answers help more than changing the subject.' He paused. 'If it keeps going or worries you, we can talk again, and the doctor too.' She let go of the strap. 'So I don't have to stop him?' 'You can just sit with him.'

qa.q: Where did Abhinav's mother find him burying his toy car?
qa.a: She found him burying it in a flowerpot.

qa.q: What does the mother twisting her bag strap suggest?
qa.a: She is anxious and afraid that her son's repeated questions and play mean something is wrong.

qa.q: What advice did Mr Irfan give, and why does it help?
qa.a: To give short, honest, patient answers rather than distract him, because repeating and playing is how children make sense of a loss.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel if his mother kept changing the subject instead?
qa.a: He might feel his questions are wrong or scary, and be left more alone and confused with his grief.

grounding: A mother worries about her grieving son's repeated questions and burial play, and a counsellor explains it is usually normal and honest answers help.

passage: I'm Sunaina, and I'm writing down what I've seen in Vikas since his Dadu died, because I'm scared I'm missing something. Every evening at seven, the time Dadu used to call, he checks my phone. Twice this week he asked, 'But where exactly is Dadu now?' I said, 'He died, beta. His body stopped, and he can't come back.' He nodded, then asked again the next day. Yesterday I saw him make a garland of paper flowers and lay it on Dadu's chair. I don't know what goes on in his head. At first I tried distracting him with cartoons. It didn't help. Now I just answer, simply, every time he asks. He seems calmer afterwards.

qa.q: What time does Vikas check his mother's phone every evening?
qa.a: At seven, the time Dadu used to call.

qa.q: Why is Sunaina scared, and what shows it?
qa.a: She worries his repeated questions and garland-making mean something is wrong; she even writes it all down in case she's missing something.

qa.q: Which approach seems to help Vikas more, and why?
qa.a: Answering simply and honestly every time, rather than distracting him with cartoons, because it lets him make sense of the loss and he seems calmer afterwards.

qa.q: What might Vikas be looking for when he checks the phone at seven?
qa.a: He may half-expect Dadu's call, a sign that he is still searching and slowly learning the calls won't come 🤍.

grounding: A mother records her grieving son's repeated questions and ritual play, fears it is unhealthy, and finds short honest answers help more than distraction.
